subject: forensic-medicine
title: Cobra and Viper Bites, Antivenom and Scorpion Sting

steps.title: Colubrine versus viperine venom
steps.tx: Snake venoms divide by dominant action in **colubrine and viperine venom**. Elapid venom of cobra and krait is mainly neurotoxic, attacking respiratory and cardiac centres with curare like neuromuscular blockade. Viperine venom is mainly haemolytic, dissolving vessel walls, haemolysing blood and depressing coagulation into a defibrinated syndrome. Sea snake venom is myotoxic. Every venom shares hyaluronidase, the spreading factor, and proteolytic enzymes are rich in crotalid, lesser in viper and almost absent in elapid venoms.
steps.say: Elapids paralyse, vipers bleed, sea snakes dissolve muscle, and hyaluronidase spreads every venom through tissue.

steps.title: Cobra bite: ptosis is the earliest sign
steps.tx: **Cobra bite** starts locally in six to eight minutes with a small reddish wheal, tender slight radiating burning pain and oozing of bloodstained fluid, swelling minimal or absent. Systemic symptoms follow in about thirty minutes: sleepiness, intoxication, leg weakness and reluctance to move. **Ptosis is the earliest neuroparalytic manifestation**, then ophthalmoplegia, then paralysis of lower limbs spreading to trunk and head, face, palate, tongue and vocal cords, with salivation and vomiting, until paralysis completes in about two hours and respiration arrests.
steps.say: A reddish wheal, then sleepiness, then drooping eyelids first: cobra paralysis climbs to the diaphragm in about two hours.

steps.tx: A **cobra bite** starts locally within six to eight minutes as a small reddish wheal, with tender radiating burning pain, oozing bloodstained fluid, and little or no swelling. Around thirty minutes later the patient is sleepy and unsteady, with weak legs and little wish to move. Ptosis is the earliest neuroparalytic manifestation, followed by ophthalmoplegia, then paralysis climbing from the legs to trunk, head, face, palate, tongue, and vocal cords, with salivation and vomiting. Paralysis is often complete in about two hours, and respiration then stops.
steps.say: A cobra bite leaves a small reddish wheal and little swelling, then sleepiness within about half an hour. Drooping lids come before the eyes stop moving and paralysis climbs to the muscles of breathing, often within two hours.

vis.alt: Both eyelids droop, and the eyes fail to move fully, in neuroparalysis after a cobra bite.
vis.caption: Ptosis and ophthalmoplegia are obvious as the patient tries to open the eyes and look ahead. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.title: Krait bite: painless, drowsy, abdominal
steps.tx: **Krait bite** resembles cobra bite with decisive differences: no swelling or burning pain at the site, milder convulsions, and a more intense feeling of drowsiness and intoxication, with albumin appearing in the urine. Victims bitten asleep may present with morning paralysis and severe abdominal pain that misleads surgeons. Inability to raise the head in supine position is the basic bedside test of imminent respiratory failure across neurotoxic bites, while the patient stays conscious but unable to speak.
steps.say: No local pain, deep drowsiness and a head that cannot lift off the pillow announce krait envenomation approaching the diaphragm.

steps.title: Viper bite: bleeding that will not clot
steps.tx: **Viper bite** declares itself locally: severe pain within eight minutes, red painful swelling from fifteen minutes, bloodstained discharge, persistent bleeding from the bite as a constant feature, blisters at twelve hours and swelling marching to the trunk in one to two days. Systemically come vomiting, giddiness, sweating, abdominal pain, dilated pupils unreactive to light, collapse and haemorrhagic syndrome from gums, rectum, sputum and bite, with haematuria in hours and blood that becomes defibrinated and will not clot. Russell's and hump nosed viper bites frequently end in renal failure.
steps.say: Pain in eight minutes, swelling in fifteen and blood that refuses to clot are viper bite until proved otherwise.

steps.title: The twenty minute whole blood clotting test
steps.tx: The **twenty minute whole blood clotting test** is the bedside arbiter in viper bite: a few millilitres of fresh venous blood stand undisturbed in a clean dry glass tube for twenty minutes and are then gently tilted; blood still liquid proves viper envenomation. It is repeated every six hours to judge repeat antivenom dosing, normalisation of clotting being the endpoint, then at twelve hour intervals for at least forty eight hours to catch recurring envenoming as hepatic factor recovery takes about six hours.
steps.say: Liquid blood at twenty minutes means viper venom at work, and the test repeated six hourly steers every further vial.

nodes.label: Fresh blood in clean dry tube

steps.tx: The **twenty minute whole blood clotting test** decides viper envenomation at the bedside. A few millilitres of fresh venous blood stand undisturbed in a clean dry glass tube for twenty minutes and are then tilted gently. Blood that is still liquid indicates viper venom. The test is repeated every six hours to guide further antivenom, clotting returning to normal being the endpoint, then every twelve hours for at least forty eight hours because envenoming can recur while the liver replaces clotting factors over about six hours.
steps.say: Fresh blood left in a plain glass tube for twenty minutes should clot. If it stays liquid, viper venom is active. Repeat the tilt every six hours to judge more antivenom, then twelve hourly for two days.

vis.alt: A glass tube of venous blood is tilted after twenty minutes and the blood remains liquid.
vis.caption: Whole blood that has stood twenty minutes in a clean dry glass tube fails to clot when the tube is tipped. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.title: First aid that helps and first aid that harms
steps.tx: **Snake bite first aid** is reassurance, firm pressure over the bite, pressure immobilisation with a broad firm bandage at fifty to seventy millimetres of mercury for elapid and sea snake bites, splinting the limb, cleaning with soap and water and lying the patient on one side. Pressure immobilisation is not used in viper bites for fear of local necrosis. Forbidden are local incision and suction, sucking the wound, chemicals on the wound, cautery and cryotherapy, each adding bleeding, nerve injury or sealed in poison.
steps.say: Bandage firmly, splint and transport; never incise, suck, cauterise or freeze a snake bite, and skip pressure bandage in viper bites.

steps.title: Polyvalent antivenom dosing
steps.tx: **Polyvalent antivenom**, raised in horses against cobra, common krait, Russell's viper and saw scaled viper venoms, is lyophilised, keeps potency about five years, and each vial neutralises about six to eight milligrams of venom. It works best within four hours, less at eight, doubtfully after twenty four. No test dose is given. Minimal envenomation takes five vials, moderate ten, severe ten to fifteen, children the same as adults, infused in five hundred millilitres over one hour; neurotoxic cases repeat ten vials after one hour.
steps.say: Five, ten or fifteen vials by severity, same for children, no test dose, and a second ten after an hour for neurotoxic bites.

steps.title: Fatal venom doses and fatal periods
steps.tx: Dried venom fatal doses put the species in order in **venom lethality figures**: krait six milligrams, echis eight, cobra twelve and Russell's viper fifteen, while one bite yields far more, cobra one hundred seventy to three hundred twenty five milligrams, Russell's viper one hundred thirty to two hundred fifty, krait only twenty and echis twenty to thirty five. Fatal periods run half to six hours for cobra and one to two days for vipers. More than half of venomous bites inject inadequate venom and stay mild, which observation periods respect.
steps.say: Six milligrams of krait venom can kill while a cobra carries three hundred in one bite, and half of all bites stay mild.

nodes.label: Observe twelve to twenty four hours

steps.title: Scorpion sting: one hole and a catecholamine storm
steps.tx: **Scorpion sting** leaves a single hole in the centre of a reddened area, separating it from snake bite. The venom, a clear toxalbumen more toxic weight for weight than snake venom though tiny in dose, is a potent autonomic stimulator releasing massive catecholamines from the adrenals with direct myocardial effects. Neurotoxic stings mimic cobra bite with restlessness, paralysis, arrhythmias, convulsions and death from pulmonary oedema or cardiac failure within hours, children being the real mortality risk. Specific antivenin exists; morphine is contraindicated, barbiturates control excitement.
steps.say: One central hole, a catecholamine storm and a failing heart mark scorpion sting, deadliest in children and never treated with morphine.
